title: Act I, Scene III
focus: the Witches' greetings and their pull

teacherSummary.text: On the heath the Witches hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor and 'king hereafter', and tell Banquo he will 'get kings, though thou be none.' They vanish. Ross and Angus arrive to tell Macbeth he is now Thane of Cawdor. Macbeth, startled, imagines murder ('horrible imaginings') and decides 'chance may crown me'; Banquo warns that 'instruments of darkness tell us truths' to betray us.

context.history: Prophecy was a dangerous subject: predicting a monarch's death could be treason. Banquo's line about 'instruments of darkness' reflects the period's belief that the devil tells half-truths to trap souls.

significance: The scene splits two responses to the same temptation: Banquo is wary, Macbeth is already thinking of murder. Whether the prophecy causes the crime or reveals a desire already there is the play's central question about fate and free will.
discussionQuestions: If a fortune teller's first prediction came true, would you trust the second? Why or why not?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with appearance versus reality?

items.prompt: Evaluate whether the Witches cause Macbeth's thoughts in this scene.

anchorPassages.note: Instruments of darkness and the first murderous imagining.
anchorPassages.text:
That trusted home
Might yet enkindle you unto the crown,
Besides the thane of Cawdor. But ’tis strange:
And oftentimes, to win us to our harm,
The instruments of darkness tell us truths,
Win us with honest trifles, to betray’s
In deepest consequence.
Cousins, a word, I pray you.
Aside.
Two truths are told,
As happy prologues to the swelling act
Of the imperial theme.—I thank you, gentlemen.
Aside.
This supernatural soliciting
Cannot be ill, cannot be good: if ill,
Why hath it given me earnest of success,
Commencing in a truth? I am thane of Cawdor:
If good, why do I yield to that suggestion
Whose horrid image doth unfix my hair
And make my seated heart knock at my ribs,
Against the use of nature? Present fears
Are less than horrible imaginings:
My thought, whose murder yet is but fantastical,
Shakes so my single state of man that function
Is smother’d in surmise, and nothing is
But what is not.

segments.script: Prophecy was a dangerous subject: predicting a monarch's death could be treason. Banquo's line about 'instruments of darkness' reflects the period's belief that the devil tells half-truths to trap souls. The scene splits two responses to the same temptation: Banquo is wary, Macbeth is already thinking of murder. Whether the prophecy causes the crime or reveals a desire already there is the play's central question about fate and free will. Characterization: Macbeth "starts" at the prophecy; Banquo is wary ("instruments of darkness"). Macbeth's asides reveal that he is already imagining murder. Dramatic irony: The audience knows Macbeth is Cawdor before he does; the prophecy's first part comes true at once. Diction / vocabulary: Macbeth's first line echoes the witches: "So foul and fair a day I have not seen." Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “So foul and fair a day I have not seen” slowly and put it in my own words: Returning from battle, Macbeth says he has never seen so foul and fair a day. Next, craft. I notice his words repeat the witches' "fair" and "foul" before he has even met them. The strongest word is “foul”: the word links him to the witches' upside-down world. Then, effect. Why does Macbeth's first line echo the witches? My answer: Without knowing it, Macbeth speaks the witches' language; Shakespeare hints that he is already connected to the evil that will tempt him moments later.
